Justice Department Announces Final Rule Allowing Federal Firearms Licensees to Voluntarily Use NICS for Employee Background Checks
Today, the Department of Justice announced a final rule authorizing Federal Firearms Licensees (FFLs) to voluntarily use the FBI's National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS) to conduct background checks on certain current and prospective employees.
“Firearms dealers deserve the confidence of knowing their employees are right with the law,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “This common-sense change delivers quick and clear background checks for firearms dealers based on the latest FBI information. The Trump Administration will always protect the Second Amendment and the rights of law-abiding gun owners.”
“Under the leadership of President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, this FBI will always protect the Second Amendment and the rights of law-abiding gun owners,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “This is a common-sense change that appropriately expedites and clarifies the background check process for firearms dealers, and I want to thank our partners for working with us to make it happen.”
The final rule implements a provision of the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act , which directed the Attorney General to issue these regulations. Participation is optional for FFLs and requires the written consent of the employee.
Under the final rule, an FFL may submit Firearm Handler Background Checks (FHCs) of eligible employees. Eligible employees include firearm handlers, employees of licensed manufacturers who have access to unfinished firearm components or manufacturing tools, and independent contractors or agents whose employment duties for an FFL allow them access to firearms, ammunition, or their manufacturing components. Those listed as responsible persons of FFLs are not eligible employees because they already undergo background checks through the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Until now, Department of Justice regulations prohibited FFLs from contacting NICS for any purpose other than a proposed firearm transfer.
NICS will search the same databases it does for a firearm transfer: the NICS Indices, the National Crime Information Center, and the Interstate Identification Index. The FFL will receive a NICS Transaction Number and one of three responses: "Pass," "Pending," or "Did Not Pass." FFLs will not receive any of the subject’s underlying record information. A "Did Not Pass" response does not prohibit an FFL from employing the person in a position that does not involve access to firearms or ammunition. Generally, an FFL may conduct one FHC per eligible employee every 12 months, unless the FFL has reasonable cause to believe the employee has become subject to a potentially prohibiting event. The FBI will not charge a fee for these checks.
A subject whose FHC received a "Did Not Pass" response may request the reason for the response and may appeal that response in the same manner and to the same extent as a person who is denied a firearm transfer.
The final rule addresses applicable public comments received on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that was published in December 2024. The final rule takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives will issue separate guidance to FFLs on how to document FHCs.
Jald Jensen, 73, of Panama City, and previously

DEPARTMENT OF THE TREASURY
WASHINGTON, D.C.
OFFICE OF FOREIGN ASSETS CONTROL
Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations
31 CFR part 560
GENERAL LICENSE FF-1
Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving
International Development Bank for Investment and Finance
(a) Except as provided in paragraph (b) of this general license, all transactions prohibited
by the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations, 31 CFR part 560 (ITSR), that are
ordinarily incident and necessary to the wind down of any transaction involving International
Development Bank for Investment and Finance, a.k.a. Iraq Development Bank (“Iraq
Development Bank”), or any entity in which Iraq Development Bank owns, directly or indirectly,
a 50 percent or greater interest, are authorized through 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time,
December 1, 2026, provided that any payment to a blocked person must be made into a blocked
account in accordance with the ITSR.
(b) This general license does not authorize any transactions otherwise prohibited by the
ITSR, including transactions involving any person blocked pursuant to the ITSR other than the
blocked persons described in paragraph (a) of this general license, unless separately authorized.
(c) Effective October 29, 2026, General License No. FF, dated October 15, 2026, is
replaced and superseded in its entirety by this General License No. FF-1.
__________________________
Bradley T. Smith
Director
Office of Foreign Assets Control
Dated: October 29, 2026

Kenya’s Phoebe Okowa elected to International Court of Justice
The UN has elected five judges to the International Court of Justice, including Kenya’s Phoebe Okowa, who has secured a full nine-year term starting in February 2027.
Okowa won 183 votes in the General Assembly and 13 in the Security Council. She is a professor of public international law at Queen Mary University of London and has served on the UN’s International Law Commission since 2021.
The other elected judges are Dapo Akande of the United Kingdom, François Alabrune of France, Mahmoud Daifallah Hmoud of Jordan and Rena Lee of Singapore.
The International Court of Justice, based in The Hague, settles legal disputes between states and issues advisory opinions on legal questions referred to it by authorised
Based in The Hague, the Court comprises 15 judges serving nine-year terms, with five seats coming up for election every three years.
No two judges may be nationals of the same State.
Candidates must secure an absolute majority in both the 193-member Assembly and the 15-member Council, which vote independently by secret ballot.
The veto does not apply, and multiple rounds of voting may be necessary.

claims.text: On October 29, 2026, OFAC issued Iran General License FF-1, signed by Director Bradley T. Smith, authorizing the wind down of transactions prohibited by the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR part 560) that involve International Development Bank for Investment and Finance (a.k.a. Iraq Development Bank) or any entity in which it owns, directly or indirectly, a 50 percent or greater interest, through 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time, December 1, 2026.

Effective October 29, 2026, Iran General License FF-1 replaced and superseded in its entirety General License No. FF dated October 15, 2026; under FF-1 any payment to a blocked person must be made into a blocked account in accordance with the ITSR, and the license does not authorize transactions involving any person blocked under the ITSR other than the bank and its 50-percent-or-greater-owned entities.

On October 21, 2026, OFAC issued Iran General License GG authorizing the wind down of transactions involving Karnakis and Karnakis, and Iran General License HH authorizing wind-down activities, limited safety and environmental transactions, and the offloading of cargo involving certain persons or vessels blocked on October 21, 2026.

letters.subject: Source request: OFAC Iran General License FF-1 and related designations
letters.body:
Dear US Department of Justice,

We are PLAIN., an independent, advertising-free Swiss news site reporting internationally (plain-news.ch). Our investigative desk is examining US OFAC amendments to Iran sanctions licensing, including Iran General License FF-1 of October 29, 2026, and the designations and wind-down licenses issued on October 21, 2026. This research is AI-assisted and every text is reviewed by a human editor. We would appreciate your help in clarifying the following specific points.

1. Under General License FF-1, which Iranian entities are now restricted, and does the license cover only the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance (also known as Iraq Development Bank) and entities in which it holds a direct or indirect 50 percent or greater interest?

2. How does FF-1's requirement that any payment to a blocked person be made into a blocked account in accordance with the ITSR affect international trade transactions that would otherwise fall within the authorized wind-down through 12:01 a.m. eastern standard time on December 1, 2026?

3. What specific transactions remain prohibited under FF-1, given that it does not authorize transactions involving any person blocked under the ITSR other than the bank and its 50-percent-or-greater-owned entities?

4. What is the stated basis for the October 21, 2026 SDN additions under Executive Order 13902 of Karnakis Kosmas Ioanis, Karnakis Kosmas Konstantinos, Karnakis Kosmas Sofianos, Ortega Jones Pedro, Ortega Jones Roberto, Amigoz Singapore Pte. Ltd. and Karnakis and Karnakis, and how do General Licenses GG and HH relate to those designations?

5. What was the specific effect of FF-1 replacing and superseding General License FF of October 15, 2026 in its entirety on transactions already underway?

We will publish your reply, either in full or as a summary, as you prefer. If anything we have stated is factually wrong, please tell us so that we can correct it. We would be grateful for an answer by 8 November 2026.

Sincerely,

PLAIN. Investigative desk
desk@plain-news.ch
